title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Mud — The World of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unsparing look at one of the strangest, richest, most underrated novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is a book that refuses to be summarised neatly.
There is a fortune built on dust heaps, a drowned man who isn't quite dead, a river that swallows people and sometimes gives them back.
There is savage comedy about money, devastating portraits of philanthropy gone rotten, and some of the most atmospheric prose Dickens ever wrote.
To help us unpack all of this, I have three extraordinary guests with me today.
First, Dr. Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power.
Daniel sees institutions — schools, charities, the law — not as neutral structures but as mechanisms that protect wealth and exhaust the poor.
He'll be reading Our Mutual Friend with a fierce and forensic eye.
Second, Professor James Blackstone — a legal and social historian who specialises in the real institutions that literature depicts.
James brings the context that makes a novel's world fully legible — what the law actually did, what poverty actually looked like, what it meant to be at the bottom.
And third, Ms. Caroline Woodcourt — a book critic who has been reading and re-reading Our Mutual Friend since she was a teenager.
Caroline brings us back to the experience of the text — what makes you stop, what makes you laugh, what makes you catch your breath.
She has strong opinions about which characters deserve better — and she's usually right.
Let's begin where the novel itself begins — with money, mud, and the Thames.
What strikes me immediately about this novel is that Dickens refuses the usual alibi.
In so many Victorian novels, the plot hinges on the idea that goodness will be rewarded — that virtue has its own economy.
Our Mutual Friend interrogates that assumption from the very first pages.
Take the Boffins — Noddy and Henrietta — who have spent their lives in service to a hard and exploitative master.
Dickens describes them with a precision that cuts both ways.
"The hard wrathful and sordid nature that had wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst."
That sentence is a whole theory of labour in a subordinate clause.
Maximum extraction, minimum pay — and Dickens knows exactly what he's describing.
And the remarkable thing is that the master's cruelty doesn't corrupt the Boffins — but Dickens refuses to make that a comfortable observation.
He's not saying goodness neutralises exploitation.
He's saying that moral integrity survives the system — but only just, and with enormous cost.
The line that follows is one of Dickens's most extraordinary moral pronouncements.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
There's almost a biblical cadence to that — and it's absolutely deliberate.
Dickens is insisting that what the powerful do to the powerless does not exhaust the moral story.
What gets me about that sentence is its rhythm — the comma after 'Evil,' the semicolon, and then 'but Good, never' landing like a full stop on a gravestone.
Dickens is doing something very precise with punctuation there.
He makes you pause before 'never' — makes you feel the weight of that word before you arrive at it.
And then the novel immediately complicates it — because the world of this book is not a world where goodness is safe.
Exactly — and nowhere does Dickens expose the danger more savagely than in his portrait of the school system.
Charley Hexam's school is one of the great satirical set-pieces in the novel.
Dickens's target is not ignorance — it's the hypocrisy of a system that pretends to educate while actually performing social control.
The narrator describes the whole establishment as being pervaded by — and he chooses this phrase deliberately —
"a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil was childish and innocent."
'Grimly ludicrous' — two words that shouldn't coexist and yet are absolutely perfect together.
Because the comedy of this passage is real — it's genuinely funny — and the grimness is real too.
The passage about Thomas Twopence is where I always lose it completely.
Dickens gives you this thumbnail moral fable — boy resists temptation, is rewarded with supernatural good fortune — and then adds in parentheses:
"Note, that the benefactor came to no good."
It's perfect. A parenthesis that demolishes the entire moral universe of the genre.
And what follows is even more devastating — the inclined plane of infants, the Sunday executioner and his acolyte smoothing wretched little faces.
It reads as comedy, but what it describes is institutional violence against children.
The ragged school movement in the 1860s was genuinely well-intentioned by many of its participants — and that's precisely what Dickens finds so infuriating.
Good intentions administered badly can be more damaging than indifference, because they carry the additional insult of self-congratulation.
And Dickens captures that perfectly when he describes the moral literature — where you were to do good not because it was good, but because —
"you were to make a good thing of it."
Virtue as investment strategy — a Victorian ideology Dickens despised with extraordinary consistency.
And then there's the river — which is where all of this finally becomes something darker than satire.
The Thames in this novel is not a backdrop — it is an active force.
There's a passage late in the novel — Bradley Headstone pursuing Eugene Wrayburn — where the landscape itself becomes a portent.
The sun sets, and Dickens writes:
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
'Guiltily shed' — that adverb is doing extraordinary work.
The guilt belongs not just to the act about to happen — it belongs to the whole structure of the novel's world.
That sentence stopped me completely the first time I read it.
'As we say' — that quiet appeal to shared knowledge — makes it feel inevitable rather than melodramatic.
Dickens is telling you exactly what is coming and somehow making it feel both shocking and fated.
It's worth noting that the Thames was, in the 1860s, the actual site of extreme violence and poverty — body-snatchers, drowning accidents, industrial waste.
Dickens is not reaching for gothic effect from nothing — he is literalising what Londoners knew perfectly well about their own river.
The blood mounting to Heaven is poetic — but the blood in the Thames was absolutely real.
Money extracted, virtue tested, blood in the water — we are very much inside the world of Our Mutual Friend.
We'll be returning to all of these threads as the episode goes on.
After the break, we'll turn to the characters who crowd this novel — the frauds and the genuine, the desperate and the predatory — and ask what Dickens is doing with all of them.

segments.title: The Law's Cold Logic: How Institutions Grind the Poor

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, piece by careful piece.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a deceptively simple question: what does this novel think institutions do to people?
Not what they say they do — what they actually do.
Joining me are three brilliant readers who've been living with this novel and with the world it depicts.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he is never shy about naming what he finds.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly how these institutions actually worked — and what it cost to be caught inside them.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel more times than she'd care to admit, and brings the reader's instinct for what is funny, what is devastating, and why.
Let's begin with something that looks like comedy but is actually a diagnosis: the way class pre-assigns a person's entire life before they've drawn breath.
James, you've been looking at Eugene Wrayburn's account of what he calls M. R. F. — his Most Respected Father.
Eugene delivers this account with such elegant detachment that you could almost miss how savage it is.
What Dickens is anatomising here is the absolute tyranny of primogeniture and professional appointment — the idea that a father's declaration at birth constitutes destiny.
The eldest is heir to, as Eugene puts it, the Family Embarrassments — not the Family Estate — that's already a giveaway about the actual state of affairs.
But the passage that truly earns its keep is the one about the second brother.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — Dickens earns that punchline with the patience of a craftsman.
Three words, and the entire edifice of Anglican preferment comes tumbling down.
What I love about this passage is the rhythm of it — the repeated structure, declaration then failure, declaration then failure.
Dickens builds the joke mechanically, like a clock winding up, so that when it strikes the hour, it's already funny before the punchline lands.
And Eugene tells it with that signature air of not quite caring — "M. R. F. amuses me" — which is itself a kind of armour.
He has been told, from before birth, what he is and what he's for.
The laughter is how he survives knowing that.
That armour reading is exactly right — but I want to stress what the system is actually doing here, beneath the comedy.
The father pre-assigns roles not out of love, but out of class management — maintaining the family's position within a hierarchy that requires each son to perform a designated function.
When those roles fail — the shaky pillar, the non-circumnavigating naval officer — the system doesn't collapse.
The sons absorb the failure privately.
And this is the invisible cruelty Dickens keeps returning to: the institution endures while individuals are broken by it.
That is precisely the legal reality of the period.
A man called to the bar without any real intention or aptitude for it — as Eugene clearly is — still had to pay his fees, keep his terms, be seen to inhabit the role.
The profession extracted its dues regardless of whether it provided any actual livelihood in return.
Which is a rather precise economic description of how many Victorian institutions worked.
And yet Dickens places the most piercing account of institutional damage not in the drawing rooms of the idle rich, but in the life of a child in pain.
James, you've also been thinking about Jenny Wren — and a vision she describes that is, in some ways, the novel's most extraordinary passage.
Jenny Wren is a child who has been comprehensively failed — by her father, by poverty, by a body that causes her constant pain.
The institutions that were supposed to protect children in Dickens's England — parish relief, charitable organisations, the courts — were largely ornamental for someone in her position.
And so she builds her own alternative world.
The passage where she describes the children she used to see is extraordinary — and I want to read part of it, because no summary does it justice.
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
Those children in white — they are not like the real children of the neighbours, who set up shrill noises and mocked her.
They are the children she was never allowed to be — not chilled, not anxious, not beaten.
Dickens uses her imagination to make visible what the world has stolen from her.
I find that passage almost unbearable in the best possible way.
The detail that gets me every time is: "They were not like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were never in pain."
She is describing angels — or something like them — but she describes them entirely through what she herself is.
The negative definition: not chilled, not anxious, not beaten.
She can only imagine relief as the absence of her own suffering.
That is one of the most quietly devastating sentences Dickens ever wrote.
And I think we have to hold both things at once — the genuine beauty of that vision and the indictment it carries.
Jenny's celestial children are a condemnation of every real institution that was supposed to protect her and didn't.
The tenderness of the writing is real — but it coexists with fury, and Dickens wants us to feel both.
Have patience, and we will come again — that's what the children say.
"Have patience, and we will come again."
Patience — the virtue the poor are always asked to have while the system finishes with them.
From the spiritual world of Jenny Wren to something altogether darker — the Thames underworld, where the institutions of society barely reach at all.
Daniel, you've been reading two passages that sit in very different registers — Pleasant Riderhood's portrait, and then John Harmon's terrifying account of near-drowning.
Pleasant Riderhood is one of Dickens's most underrated characters, and this passage is the reason why.
Dickens does something genuinely unusual here — he asks us to understand her predatory behaviour toward sailors not as moral failure but as trained response.
As some dogs have it in the blood, or are trained — that comparison is doing a lot of work.
She has been shaped by her environment as surely as any animal.
And then the catalogue of what she sees when she looks at ordinary social ceremonies.
"Show her a Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular licence to quarrel and fight."
A licence to quarrel — it's a legal term used against the institution of marriage, and it's perfectly precise.
Wedding, Christening, Funeral — the novel strips each ceremony down to what it actually delivers to someone at the bottom of the social order.
The Funeral passage stops me every time I read it.
An unremunerative ceremony conferring a temporary gentility — and then that sting: representing the only formal party ever given by the deceased.
These people's whole lives have contained no ceremony, no occasion, no recognition — until they die.
And yet the passage ends with something tender — a touch of romance in Pleasant, a vision of far-off islands.
She dreams of a congenial partner among groves of bread-fruit — and the novel's final joke is that even her Eden requires sailors to be got the better of.
She cannot imagine a world without the system she was made by.
There's a bitter historical accuracy to that portrait of the father — his duty always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap, and being discharged hurt her.
The word discharged is doing extraordinary double work there — legal, mechanical, and physical all at once.
A father who discharges his duty by striking his child.
That is an accurate portrait of what parental authority actually meant, legally, for much of the nineteenth century — effectively unlimited, essentially unchallengeable.
Pleasant Riderhood is not pathological — she is the product of a system that had no interest in protecting her.
And then Dickens moves us from Pleasant's Thames to John Harmon's — and the register shifts completely.
In the drowning passages, identity itself becomes the thing at stake.
It begins with the clothes — Radfoot insisting on the exchange, the black servant who brings coffee and never looks at Harmon.
Harmon recounts Radfoot's words with an eerie precision.
"You are very wet, Mr Harmon — I can hear him saying — and I am quite dry under this good waterproof coat. Put on these clothes of mine."
He is literally being persuaded out of his own identity — his own clothes — by a man who intends to kill him.
And the black servant who never looks at him — that detail is both gothic and historically charged.
Someone already at the margins of visibility is present at the moment a man's identity is erased — and witnesses nothing.
The drowning passage that follows is one of the most technically astonishing things in the novel.
Harmon addresses himself by name — which is so strange, and so right.
The prose leads into it like a descent.
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
The repetition of his own name — three times — is the novel insisting on identity as something that must be actively asserted under pressure.
And what pressure — a downward slide through something like a tube, then a great noise and sparkling and crackling as of fires.
It reads like death and resurrection at once.
And into that gothic frame Dickens slots the novel's great question: can a man unmake himself from the identity a system has assigned him?
Bradley Headstone is the shadow version of that question.
He has climbed the system — respectable schoolmaster, a man of rigidly achieved position — and the system has not freed him.
The passage where he creeps up the dark staircase outside Wrayburn's chambers is one of the most disturbing in the novel.

"If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night."
The haggard head floating up the dark staircase — Dickens disembodies him, turns him into pure murderous intention.
He has been made by the system, and the system is going to break him.
Bradley is a historically precise figure — the self-made man whose respectability is entirely performative and therefore entirely precarious.
The Victorian schoolmaster occupied an extraordinarily ambiguous social position — educated enough to instruct, but not enough to be received.
He inhabits exactly the crack in the social structure where resentment accumulates.
And Dickens understood — I think better than most social theorists of the period — that this kind of trapped mobility produces something very dangerous.

So across all of these passages — the comic futility of Eugene's assigned destiny, Jenny's visionary escape, Pleasant's trained cynicism, Harmon's near-erasure, Bradley's staircase vigil — what the novel keeps asking is whether anyone can survive the identity the system gives them.
Daniel, James, Caroline — thank you.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money — quite literally — and ask what the dust-heaps and the river actually mean as economic symbols in Our Mutual Friend.

segments.title: Bella's Education: From Mercenary to Human

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's obsession with money and identity — and nowhere does Dickens press that question harder than in the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
She begins the novel as, by her own cheerful admission, a mercenary little creature — and ends it as something far more interesting.
Today we're asking: what actually educates Bella Wilfer, and what does the novel think that education costs?
With me are Daniel Rosen, cultural historian and our resident anatomist of class power.
James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who keeps us honest about what these institutions actually were.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of the novel, who cares deeply about what it feels like to be inside these pages.
Let's begin with John Harmon — because his deception is the engine that drives Bella's transformation.
What's so striking about John Harmon's confession in that long interior monologue is how clearly Dickens names the source of his paralysis.
It isn't romantic anxiety — it's the inherited corruption of wealth itself.
Listen to how he puts it — this is Harmon cataloguing what coming home meant:

'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father's intention in thrusting that marriage on me.'
Every verb there is a recoil — shrinking, mistrustful, afraid.
This is a man deformed by the very thing he's about to inherit.
And the mechanism he invents to escape that deformation — the disguise, the test — is itself a product of the same diseased logic.
And what I find so painful — and so honest — is that Dickens doesn't let Harmon off easily with that logic.
There's a passage in the next chapter where Dickens traces exactly how the 'harmless' deception metastasised.
The language is extraordinarily precise about self-deception.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Never yet for good within his knowledge then' — that parenthesis is everything.
The wealth has never done good — that is presented as simple fact, not sentiment.
And yet somehow this man who knows that is going to inherit it all and try to make it otherwise.
There is something worth pausing on in the practical architecture of Harmon's scheme, because it is not merely romantic fantasy.
He and Radfoot dress as common sailors — specifically common sailors — and place themselves in Bella's neighbourhood.
The text is quite explicit about it:
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
Now in the mid-Victorian period, a sailor dressing down for the East End would have been entirely unremarkable.
What Harmon is actually doing is purchasing a kind of freedom — freedom to observe without the distorting lens of his own wealth and name.
The disguise is, at its root, a fantasy of escaping class — dressed up as love.
James is absolutely right that it's a class fantasy — but I'd push that further.
The fantasy is available only to someone who already possesses the wealth he's pretending to have escaped.
The poor man in sailors' clothes is simply a poor man in sailors' clothes.
He has no fortune waiting to vindicate his virtue.
And the novel knows this — which is part of why Dickens plants the passage about Bella's dilemma so carefully.
Harmon sees that to come to life and accept the inheritance means buying Bella — and to come to life and reject it means punishing her.
The money corrupts every transaction — including the apparently selfless ones.

I want to bring in something that sits alongside all of this — because the novel offers a kind of dark counterpoint to Bella's education in the figure of the little alcoholic child that Lizzie describes.
It's a brief passage, but it's devastating.
Lizzie is explaining the child's history to Charley, and she says:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
'If she ever had one' — that afterthought is almost unbearable.
Bella has her peculiarities and her mercenary wishes — but she had a cradle.
She had the material conditions that make moral transformation even possible.
That point strikes me as exactly right — and historically it's not a metaphor, it's a description.
Children in the industrial slums of mid-Victorian London genuinely were given gin to quiet them.
The father in this passage — 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — is not a Dickensian caricature.
That is a perfectly accurate portrait of industrial alcoholism in the 1860s.
What's quietly radical about Dickens here is the parenthetical Lizzie adds: 'But a good workman too, at the work he does.'
He insists on seeing the labour even inside the ruin.
And that, for me, is where the novel's real radicalism lives — not in the romance of Bella's transformation, but in those asides.
Bella gets a fully orchestrated education — the Boffin household, Harmon's patient test, the gradual stripping away of her mercenary self-image.
That child surrounded by drunkards — she gets nothing.
The novel sees that injustice — it frames it with quiet precision — and then it moves on.
Because the plot requires Bella to be saved, and plots, like money, are not distributed equally.
I don't entirely disagree — but I think there's a scene that complicates the comfortable cynicism, and it involves Mr Boffin.
There's a wonderful moment where Boffin tears apart the whole performance of charity — the endless lists of patrons and patronesses.
He's talking about the correspondence piling up on Rokesmith's desk, and he says:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
It's brilliant comic writing — but it's also moral argument delivered at full gallop.
Boffin — the dustman's heir — sees through the charity machinery more clearly than anyone.
And part of Bella's education is being in that household, breathing that air.
The satire on charitable patronage is very precise, historically speaking.
By the 1860s the proliferation of charitable societies in London was extraordinary — and the title inflation Boffin mocks was entirely real.
Five shillings bought you a printed name in a list that would sit on a gentleman's side table and signal his benevolence to visitors.
It was philanthropy as social advertisement — and Dickens via Boffin identifies it as 'stark staring impudence.'
What's instructive for Bella is that the money she once worshipped is being shown to her as genuinely ridiculous.
So we've traced the education from multiple directions — the trap Harmon built, the moral luck Bella had that others didn't, and the Boffin household as its own kind of corrective institution.
What strikes me listening to all of you is how much the novel's warmth toward Bella coexists with a very cold accounting of what made her transformation possible.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the river and the dust heaps — the novel's two great symbols of value recirculating in a corrupt economy.

segments.title: The Music of Dickens: Reading for Laughter and Heart

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's final completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with full attention to every strange and brilliant corner of it.
I'm your host, and with me today are three people whose company I'd want in any reading group.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he's the person who reminds you that every drawing room in Dickens is also a battlefield.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world into the reading — the actual institutions, the actual law, what poverty actually meant.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and cares, above all, about what it's like to read it — what makes you laugh, what stops you cold.
This segment is about Dickens the comedian and the craftsman — the verbal music, the dark jokes, the moments where the prose does something so strange you have to read it twice.
Caroline, you're the natural person to open this up — where do you want to start?
I want to start with the Lammles — because Dickens does something there that I think is genuinely uncanny.
The Lammles are performing their affectionate marriage for the benefit of everyone around them, and the narrator watches with this absolutely deadpan relish.
And then he pivots into something that crosses comedy and genuine gothic horror — listen to this.
"How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out 'Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'"
That word — suffocating — is doing so much work.
It's funny in an absurdist way, the skeleton helpfully announcing itself.
But it's also — and I mean this seriously — a little terrifying, this image of something alive and gasping behind a social performance.
The phrase 'the skeleton in the closet' was already a well-worn figure of speech by the eighteen-sixties, which is precisely why Dickens literalizes it so brutally.
The Lammles' secret is financial fraud — they've each married the other believing the other to be wealthy.
That's the social reality: a marriage market so corrupted that two people can conduct a mutually fraudulent transaction and call it a wedding.
What the skeleton is 'suffocating' on, if you want to press the metaphor, is the atmosphere of respectable society itself.
That's not a small joke — that's a verdict on the whole system.
James is right, and I'd push even further.
The humor is the critique — they're not separable.
The joke only lands because every reader in Dickens's audience had sat in a drawing room and performed exactly the same thing the Lammles are performing.
Dickens makes you laugh at the Lammles, and in doing so, you are laughing at yourself — at the entire economy of social pretence that holds bourgeois society together.
That's the radical move — satire as mirror, not just weapon.
And when Dickens turns to comedy that is more purely comic — when he lets himself be properly funny — the writing becomes even more precise, not less.
The Wegg scenes are the best example in the whole novel, I think.
There's a moment where Wegg is on the outside of a door, and Boffin is on the inside, and Dickens gives us this.
"This time Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
'Laboured with a will' — it's a completely serious description of a completely absurd action.
And 'laughed silently' — that is terrifying, actually.
Wegg enjoying his power over Boffin, alone in the dark, laughing to himself — that's not just funny, that's menacing.
The grindstone is perfect because it's a working-class implement being deployed as an instrument of class blackmail.
Wegg is a man with almost nothing — a wooden leg, a street stall — who has found a lever over the wealthy Boffin.
The mime of grinding — this imaginary labour — is Wegg fantasising about the kind of power he's never had.
Dickens lets him have this grotesque little triumph, and then the novel takes it away — spectacularly.
Which is where Sloppy comes in.
And before Sloppy, there's the Secretary — who delivers one of the most satisfying lines in the novel.
Wegg is making his usual insolent overtures, and the Secretary simply tells him:
"Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it."
'Or I will throw you after it.' Full stop.
No raised voice, no elaboration — the threat is entirely credible precisely because it's so calm.
That's a technique Dickens uses throughout — the controlled understatement that is, in fact, the most powerful possible statement.
And then Sloppy — glorious Sloppy — delivers on the promise.
The passage describing what he does to Wegg is one I have read aloud to people who had never touched this novel, and they laugh every single time.
Dickens writes:
"Sloppy lightly trotted out with him and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street door."

"Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents."
"A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash."
'A prodigious splash.' That's a complete sentence, and it's the funniest sentence in the chapter.
Dickens saves it — puts it alone — so it lands like a dropped weight.
What I love about that scene — and I'll admit 'love' is not a word I often deploy — is that the justice is administered by Sloppy.
Sloppy, who was raised in a workhouse, who has no status, no property, no claim to anything the novel's society values.
And Wegg — who has spent the entire novel trying to leverage his tiny scrap of literacy into power over a richer man — ends up in a rubbish cart.
The dust returns to dust — but Dickens makes it funny rather than grim, and that choice is itself a moral argument.
There's a legal satisfaction to it as well — Wegg had been running an extortion scheme, essentially.
The novel can't quite put him on trial — the circumstances are too murky — so Sloppy's arms are the only court available.
And that tells you something true about the period — formal justice was not available to those without resources, and informal justice was often the only kind that worked.
Dickens knew that, and the comedy is the vehicle for saying it.
That image — of Sloppy as the novel's last available court of justice — is going to stay with me.
What we've seen in this segment is that for Dickens, comedy and critique are the same instrument — played with extraordinary precision.
Coming up: we're going to look at how the novel handles money itself — not just greed, but the strange, almost magical way wealth moves through this world.
Stay with us.

segments.title: John Harmon's Secret: Plot, Identity, and the Novel's Machinery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see what's inside.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in the novel's opening machinery: the question of who John Harmon is, and what the world he's returned to actually costs its inhabitants.
With me today are three exceptional readers of this novel, each bringing a completely different lens.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as an anatomy of class power — he will find the economic nerve running through every scene.
Prof James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions looked like from the inside — the law, the dust trade, the money.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a literary critic and devoted re-reader of this novel who cares passionately about what the prose actually does on the page.
Welcome, all three of you.
We begin with the novel's social world — and specifically a man named Twemlow, who may be the most brilliantly humiliating metaphor in all of Dickens.
Twemlow is one of those moments where Dickens stops being a novelist and becomes a satirist of almost savage precision.
He introduces this character — a man of gentle birth, connected to the aristocracy — as, and I want to be exact here, a piece of dinner-furniture.
An innocent piece of furniture on easy castors, kept in storage when not in use.
What Dickens is describing — with that lethal calm — is the complete instrumentalisation of a human being by the class system.
Twemlow's only value is his proximity to Lord Snigsworth — his social utility, his ability to lend legitimacy to the Veneerings' table.
And the cruelest detail is this: the more he is needed, the more leaves are added, the further he is pushed from the centre.
What gets me every time is that Dickens commits to the metaphor entirely — he never winks at us.
The logic of the dining table is followed through with complete mechanical seriousness.
He sets up the quote so beautifully — and then you get this:
He represents the dining-table in its normal state.
That phrase — its normal state — is quietly devastating.
Twemlow is not a person in this social world — he is the baseline condition of a respectable dinner party.
The detail about the livery stable-yard is doing more work than it might appear.
A man of Twemlow's connection — a first cousin to a peer — occupying rooms above a stable yard is a very precise social signal.
He has the lineage but not the money, which makes him exactly the kind of figure the Veneerings can exploit — title without wealth is a commodity they can rent.
The Veneerings, of course, have the inverse problem: money without social standing.
Dickens understood that arrangement with remarkable sociological clarity, whatever else one might say about him.
James is right, and it connects directly to the Harmon inheritance — the money that everyone in this novel orbits around like a dark star.
What's striking about the Boffins' testimony to Lightwood is how it reveals Old Harmon's cruelty as a kind of domestic economy.
He withholds even a sixpence of coach-money from a child being sent abroad.
And when Mrs Boffin dared to speak about the natural affections — dared, in his own household — listen to what Boffin describes:
That repetition — Dropped her — is Boffin unable to find any other words for it.
The violence of property — Old Harmon defending his right to be cruel to his own son — is completely exposed in that single bonnet spinning across the yard.
That passage is extraordinary — and what makes it land is the parenthesis about the bonnet.
She wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head.
That digression is Boffin's voice — warm, precise, slightly bewildered — making the violence more real by surrounding it with the ordinary.
And then the other memory — the child being sent away.
Boffin describes the scene at the fire — Mrs Boffin warming the boy's cheeks — and it builds very quietly to this:
The reduplication — wide wide world — is doing everything.
It's how a woman speaks when ordinary language isn't large enough.
The legal context here is worth a moment.
Old Harmon's power over his son was effectively absolute — a father could disinherit, dispatch, and legally abandon a child with very little recourse available to anyone.
The Boffins' repeated interventions on young John's behalf were acts of genuine moral courage, not sentiment.
There was nothing they could do legally — they could only stand between the boy and the old man and take the consequences.
Which, in Mrs Boffin's case, meant a bonnet spinning across the yard and a blow to the temple.
And then the fortune arrives — and the Boffins are left trying to make something redemptive out of it.
Mrs Boffin's proposal to Boffin is one of the most quietly radical moments in the novel's opening.
She wants to find an orphan child, name him John Harmon, and provide for him — to use the dead boy's money in the dead boy's name.
Now that he is past all benefit of the money — the money he should have inherited — she wants to give his name to someone else who has nothing.
It's a gesture that quietly indicts the entire system of inheritance — the money should have been his, and now it can only impersonate him.
And of course the irony is savage — because John Harmon isn't dead.
He's in the novel, disguised, watching all of this unfold.
Mrs Boffin wants to resurrect him in a borrowed child, and the real man is standing somewhere nearby, unable to announce himself.
Dickens constructs the whole novel on that terrible and tender irony.
Which brings us to Bella Wilfer — the other person caught in the machinery of the Harmon will.
She was named in the will as the intended bride of a man she had never met, which is itself a remarkable legal and moral grotesquerie.
And by the time we reach her in the Boffin household, she is undergoing a kind of corruption — absorbing their money, their comfort, and Boffin's increasingly acquisitive philosophy.
The scene in her room — Bella at the mirror — is one of the novel's most uncomfortable moments precisely because Dickens makes her self-awareness part of the problem.
She knows what she's doing — she knows that Boffin's money-worship mirrors her own desires — and she still can't stop.
Listen to how she interrogates herself:
Inconsistent little Beast — she calls herself that in the looking-glass, and the comedy barely covers the distress.
The looking-glass is the novel's little emblem for self-examination that produces no change — she sees herself clearly and does nothing.
What I find remarkable is the phrase liberal benefactor — she uses Boffin's own generosity as the charge against herself.
He has given her everything, she knows it, and she still finds him contemptible for saying out loud what she privately believes.
That is a very precise portrait of a particular kind of moral cowardice — to hold a value secretly while despising those who hold it openly.
Dickens is not being cruel to Bella — he is being absolutely honest.
That phrase — inconsistent little Beast — seems like a good place to pause, because it captures something this novel returns to again and again.
The characters who see themselves most clearly are not thereby freed — they're simply more eloquent witnesses to their own entanglement.
In our next segment, we'll follow that thread further — into the river, and the money, and the question of what it might mean to be redeemed by inheritance.

segments.title: Dust, Wealth, and Rot: The Boffins and the Corruption of Gold

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've arrived at one of the novel's great dark comedies: the moment when money pours in, and the vultures descend.
The Boffins — Noddy and Henrietta — are decent people, genuinely good-hearted.
And Dickens asks: what happens to decency when it is suddenly very, very rich?
To unpick that question we have three guides today.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class power, and he brings forensic precision to everything Dickens touches.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows what the institutions Dickens lampoons actually looked like from the inside.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is the reader who loves this novel most fiercely, and listens hardest to the prose.
Let's begin with the Boffins themselves — who they are, and what Dickens quietly does to them from the very start.
What strikes me first about the Boffins is that Dickens refuses to let their goodness be fashionable.
There is a tiny devastating scene — just two sentences — where Boffin simply tells his wife he's glad she's his wife.
Listen to what Dickens does with that tenderness.
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And then — immediately — the narrator steps in with the verdict.
'It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
That capital U on Unfashionable is not accidental — Dickens is stamping them with it like a brand.
In the Victorian social order, respectability was a performance — and the Boffins are constitutionally incapable of performing it.
Dickens loves them for it, but the novel also shows exactly how that guilelessness makes them targets.
That word 'hopelessly' does something quite specific to the reader.
It sounds like criticism — and then you realise it isn't, not quite.
It's the narrator pretending to be society, and then winking at you over society's shoulder.
The Boffins are unfashionable in the same way that bread is unfashionable — it's just real, and it sustains you.
And yet Dickens sets them up in a world where being real is a liability.
James is right that they're targets — but I want to press on what the targeting actually looks like.
Because Dickens gives us a brilliant catalogue of the machinery that descends on anyone who is publicly, visibly wealthy.
The chapter on the Secretary reading the Boffins' mail is one of the most savage satirical inventories in Victorian fiction.
Dickens gives us the Duke of Linseed — and here's the key move.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
The adjective 'fat' is doing extraordinary work there — it makes the letter itself a body, and a bloated one.
The aristocracy presents itself as conferring honour, but Dickens strips it to what it is: a lithographed form letter, sent by the hundred.
The steward's fee is three guineas.
The whole edifice of aristocratic condescension — and the price is three guineas.
And this is historically precise — the Victorian charity dinner circuit was genuinely structured this way.
You bought your stewardship, your name went on the printed list, and the institution skimmed the difference.
What Dickens captures is that charity, in this world, is primarily a mechanism for the movement of money upward.
The noble earls and the viscount combined to solicit Boffin — and the passage just drips with controlled contempt.
Dickens notes the letter is 'lithographed by the hundred' — it barely bothers with the pretence of personal address.
Boffin is not a person to these people — he is a notated sum.
Then Dickens moves from the corporate beggars to the individual ones — and the register shifts.
It becomes almost unbearably funny and then quietly tragic within the same paragraph.
There's a line about the documents these individual beggars enclose that I have to read aloud.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That is such a Dickens simile — precise, grotesque, and slightly cruel.
But then he gives us the 'beggars of punctual business-habits' — those who will 'be cold in death' at a quarter to one on Tuesday if no money arrives.
And you laugh — and then you stop laughing, because these are people in genuine desperation performing desperation for an audience of one.
That's exactly it — they've been forced to commodify their own misery.
The market has reached all the way into their suffering and turned it into a pitch, a product.
The 'nobly independent beggars' who 'ever regarded gold as dross' — that's Dickens skewering the ideology of genteel poverty precisely.
They want a loan — interest at five percent — and if you refuse, they will despise you.
The audacity is the point — it's what the system produces.
And Boffin, the Golden Dustman, sits at the centre of this hurricane of need and greed as a kind of passive magnet.
The dust heaps didn't corrupt him — but the fact of wealth creates its own gravitational field of corruption around him.
Which brings us to the figures who are not merely appealing to Boffin, but actively scheming against him.
Silas Wegg and Mr Venus — a literary man and a taxidermist, which is itself a kind of Dickensian joke about the art of constructing the dead.
They have found a will — an earlier will — that they believe could dispossess Boffin entirely.
James, what does that will actually say?
Wegg reads it out with barely concealed delight, and the terms are extraordinary.
Here is the crux of the document, as Wegg delivers it.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him' — the contempt in that phrase is remarkable.
John Harmon senior had so much bitterness toward his dependants that even in death he wanted to circumscribe them.
And legally, what Wegg holds is genuine leverage — a testamentary instrument, properly executed and witnessed.
In Victorian law, a later will supersedes an earlier one — but only if the later will is known to exist and can be proved valid.
Wegg understands this perfectly, and what he proposes next is a masterpiece of grubby extortion.
And the language Wegg uses to describe his scheme is a parody of the language of capital.
He calls Boffin 'the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour' — but he also speaks of their 'comrade, brother, and partner' — it's grotesque corporate fraternity.
And the plan itself — it's worth hearing exactly how Dickens renders it.
'He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
And if Boffin is caught taking anything from the Mounds — anything at all —
'he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
Moral bondage and slavery — in the mouth of a man extorting a former servant.
Dickens knows exactly what he is doing with that language — these are the words of chattel slavery applied to a property dispute between small men.
The dust heaps have made everyone in their orbit think in the same degraded terms: possession, extraction, ownership of persons.
What I find almost unbearable about the Wegg scenes is the comedy — because you cannot stop it from being funny.
He opens the extortion proposal to correction — perhaps it should be two-thirds, perhaps three-fourths, he's 'ever open' to revision.
He's like a man haggling at a market stall, except the stall is another man's life.
And against the warmth of those early scenes with the Boffins — that contented, unfashionable pair — this scheming feels especially cold.
Dickens has made us love them so that their beleaguerment hurts.
That tension — between the novel's warmth toward the Boffins and the cold machinery closing in around them — sits at the heart of what makes this strand of the book so powerful.
Dust, gold, inheritance, extortion — Dickens weaves them all into the same question about what wealth does to people and what people do to each other for it.
Thank you — Daniel, James, Caroline — that was a rich and bracing dig through the Mounds.
In our next segment, we turn to another form of corruption — the drawing rooms of Society, where a different kind of dust settles.

segments.title: Closing: What Dickens Knew About Power

utterances.text: We've been circling something throughout this conversation — a question about what kind of novelist Dickens finally was.
Not just a chronicler of poverty, not just a sentimentalist, but someone who understood how power actually works.
Daniel, I want to give you the floor to bring these threads together — because I think the three passages you've been sitting with all evening speak directly to that question.
What Dickens understood — and this is easy to miss if you're reading too quickly — is that shame is not a private feeling.
It is something the system manufactures and deposits in people so that they police themselves.
Look at what Lizzie Hexam says — and this is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the whole novel.
'I, with poor father's grave not even cleared of undeserved stain and shame, and he trying to clear it for me! I a lady!'
She uses the word 'undeserved' — she knows the stain is false — and yet it stops her cold.
That is what a class system does at its most efficient: it makes the injustice feel like a personal failing.
And what makes it so unbearable is the repetition — 'I a lady!' — twice, with that low voice and her eyes on the fire.
Dickens gives her no interlocutor in that moment. She's talking to herself. She's been so thoroughly taught her place that she argues herself back into it.
And you feel, as a reader, that furious helplessness — because you can see exactly what she cannot.
What Daniel is describing in Lizzie has its institutional twin in the Deputy Lock scene — and that one works rather differently, because Dickens is in a more satirical register.
The official pockets Betty Higden's coins one by one — the detail of 'one by one' is exquisite — and simultaneously delivers himself of his moral credentials.
Dickens writes it so that you see him perform the gesture of wiping his brow — as if the coins were the fruit of honest toil.
'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow... and I won't stand in your way. Go where you like.'
Go where you like — from a man who has just extracted what he can from an old woman fleeing the workhouse. The freedom on offer is the freedom to be nobody's problem.
That's precisely it. The language of liberty — 'go where you like' — deployed as a mechanism of abandonment.
And Dickens has the gall — the genius — to frame this as comedy. The sleeve drawn across the brow. The pantomime of honest labour.
Because the institutions of Victorian welfare were theatrical in exactly this way — they performed benevolence while extracting compliance.
And then — and this is what I find remarkable — Dickens turns around and gives us the Bella and John supper scene.
Because the novel's critique of the system is not simply that it makes people miserable. It is that it robs them of this.
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
The most delicious meal any of them had ever had — eaten in a counting-house, surrounded by brass safe-knobs staring like a dull dragon.
The system is right there in the room, and joy happens anyway. That is Dickens's argument for human resilience — and it is a serious one.
The nursery hobgoblin comparison is such a Dickensian move — it's playful, it's Bella's voice you're hearing, it's warm.
But underneath it is this rather startling domestic fact: that poverty had made even ordinary pleasure inaccessible to all three of them.
'By far the most delicious' — those five words carry the weight of every meal that was not enough.
And it's worth noting where that supper is happening — in Veneering's counting-house, with the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles watching over them.
The machinery of commerce literally frames the moment of grace. Dickens is not letting us forget the context, even in his most tender scenes.
That, for me, is what makes him more than a moralist. He is a diagnostician who also, somehow, holds out hope.
A diagnostician who holds out hope. I think that might be the finest description of Dickens I've heard in a long time.
Shame internalised by Lizzie Hexam. Liberty weaponised by a corrupt official. Joy surviving inside the counting-house.
Three images from Our Mutual Friend — and together they tell you almost everything about what Dickens knew about power.
My warmest thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has, I think, done real justice to a very great novel.
We'll be back with more episodes of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — and until then, keep reading slowly.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c18:p1.text:
It was a school for all ages, and for both sexes. The latter were kept
      apart, and the former were partitioned off into square assortments. But,
      all the place was pervaded by a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil
      was childish and innocent. This pretence, much favoured by the
      lady-visitors, led to the ghastliest absurdities. Young women old in the
      vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves
      enthralled by the good child’s book, the Adventures of Little Margery, who
      resided in the village cottage by the mill; severely reproved and morally
      squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty; divided her
      porridge with singing birds; denied herself a new nankeen bonnet, on the
      ground that the turnips did not wear nankeen bonnets, neither did the
      sheep who ate them; who plaited straw and delivered the dreariest orations
      to all comers, at all sorts of unseasonable times. So, unwieldy young
      dredgers and hulking mudlarks were referred to the experiences of Thomas
      Twopence, who, having resolved not to rob (under circumstances of uncommon
      atrocity) his particular friend and benefactor, of eighteenpence,
      presently came into supernatural possession of three and sixpence, and
      lived a shining light ever afterwards. (Note, that the benefactor came to
      no good.) Several swaggering sinners had written their own biographies in
      the same strain; it always appearing from the lessons of those very
      boastful persons, that you were to do good, not because it  was  good, but
      because you were to make a good thing of it. Contrariwise, the adult
      pupils were taught to read (if they could learn) out of the New Testament;
      and by dint of stumbling over the syllables and keeping their bewildered
      eyes on the particular syllables coming round to their turn, were as
      absolutely ignorant of the sublime history, as if they had never seen or
      heard of it. An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a
      school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white,
      jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night. And particularly
      every Sunday night. For then, an inclined plane of unfortunate infants
      would be handed over to the prosiest and worst of all the teachers with
      good intentions, whom nobody older would endure. Who, taking his stand on
      the floor before them as chief executioner, would be attended by a
      conventional volunteer boy as executioner’s assistant. When and where it
      first became the conventional system that a weary or inattentive infant in
      a class must have its face smoothed downward with a hot hand, or when and
      where the conventional volunteer boy first beheld such system in
      operation, and became inflamed with a sacred zeal to administer it,
      matters not. It was the function of the chief executioner to hold forth,
      and it was the function of the acolyte to dart at sleeping infants,
      yawning infants, restless infants, whimpering infants, and smooth their
      wretched faces; sometimes with one hand, as if he were anointing them for
      a whisker; sometimes with both hands, applied after the fashion of
      blinkers. And so the jumble would be in action in this department for a
      mortal hour; the exponent drawling on to My Dearert Childerrenerr, let us
      say, for example, about the beautiful coming to the Sepulchre; and
      repeating the word Sepulchre (commonly used among infants) five hundred
      times, and never once hinting what it meant; the conventional boy
      smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole
      hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes,
      whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in
      High Market for the purpose.
c18:p1.summary: The narrator satirizes the school's pretense of innocence, the unsuitable moral literature forced on corrupt pupils, and the brutal Sunday school system where teachers violently 'smooth' inattentive children.
c18:p1.best_quote: An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.

c51:p62.text:
The boat went on, under the arching trees, and over their tranquil shadows
      in the water. The bargeman skulking on the opposite bank of the stream,
      went on after it. Sparkles of light showed Riderhood when and where the
      rower dipped his blades, until, even as he stood idly watching, the sun

c51:p62.summary: As Bradley pursues Eugene into the fading light, the reddening landscape evokes blood guiltily shed, mounting to heaven—a foreshadowing of tragic violence.

‘Perfectly so, believe me; and with every sentiment of affectionate
      deference towards M. R. F. But if he amuses me, I can’t help it. When my
      eldest brother was born, of course the rest of us knew (I mean the rest of
      us would have known, if we had been in existence) that he was heir to the
      Family Embarrassments—we call it before the company the Family
      Estate. But when my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, “this,”
       says M. R. F., “is a little pillar of the church.”  Was  born, and became a
      pillar of the church; a very shaky one. My third brother appeared,
      considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother; but M. R. F., not
      at all put out by surprise, instantly declared him a Circumnavigator. Was
      pitch-forked into the Navy, but has not circumnavigated. I announced
      myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied
      before you. When my younger brother was half an hour old, it was settled
      by M. R. F. that he should have a mechanical genius. And so on. Therefore
      I say that M. R. F. amuses me.’
c12:p25.summary: Eugene recounts how his father pre-arranged careers for all his siblings (eldest as heir, second as clergyman, third as naval officer, himself as barrister and married man, youngest as mechanical genius), all with varying degrees of failure.
c12:p25.best_quote: When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, "this," says M. R. F., "is a little pillar of the church." Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one.

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.
c19:p76.best_quote: 'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'

c29:p3.text:
As some dogs have it in the blood, or are trained, to worry certain
      creatures to a certain point, so—not to make the comparison
      disrespectfully—Pleasant Riderhood had it in the blood, or had been
      trained, to regard seamen, within certain limits, as her prey. Show her a
      man in a blue jacket, and, figuratively speaking, she pinned him
      instantly. Yet, all things considered, she was not of an evil mind or an
      unkindly disposition. For, observe how many things were to be considered
      according to her own unfortunate experience. Show Pleasant Riderhood a
      Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular
      licence to quarrel and fight. Show her a Christening, and she saw a little
      heathen personage having a quite superfluous name bestowed upon it,
      inasmuch as it would be commonly addressed by some abusive epithet: which
      little personage was not in the least wanted by anybody, and would be
      shoved and banged out of everybody’s way, until it should grow big enough
      to shove and bang. Show her a Funeral, and she saw an unremunerative
      ceremony in the nature of a black masquerade, conferring a temporary
      gentility on the performers, at an immense expense, and representing the
      only formal party ever given by the deceased. Show her a live father, and
      she saw but a duplicate of her own father, who from her infancy had been
      taken with fits and starts of discharging his duty to her, which duty was
      always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap, and being
      discharged hurt her. All things considered, therefore, Pleasant Riderhood
      was not so very, very bad. There was even a touch of romance in her—of
      such romance as could creep into Limehouse Hole—and maybe sometimes
      of a summer evening, when she stood with folded arms at her shop-door,
      looking from the reeking street to the sky where the sun was setting, she
      may have had some vaporous visions of far-off islands in the southern seas
      or elsewhere (not being geographically particular), where it would be good
      to roam with a congenial partner among groves of bread-fruit, waiting for
      ships to be wafted from the hollow ports of civilization. For, sailors to
      be got the better of, were essential to Miss Pleasant’s Eden.
c29:p3.summary: Despite her predatory nature toward sailors and cynical views of life's ceremonies and relationships shaped by abuse, Pleasant Riderhood retains romantic dreams of escaping to distant islands.
c29:p3.best_quote: Show her a Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular licence to quarrel and fight.

‘He had carried under his arm a canvas bag, containing a suit of his
      clothes. I had no change of outer clothes with me, as I was to buy slops.
      “You are very wet, Mr Harmon,”—I can hear him saying—“and I am
      quite dry under this good waterproof coat. Put on these clothes of mine.
      You may find on trying them that they will answer your purpose to-morrow,
      as well as the slops you mean to buy, or better. While you change, I’ll
      hurry the hot coffee.” When he came back, I had his clothes on, and there
      was a black man with him, wearing a linen jacket, like a steward, who put
      the smoking coffee on the table in a tray and never looked at me. I am so
      far literal and exact? Literal and exact, I am certain.

‘It was only after a downward slide through something like a tube, and

c44:p10.text:
The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended

      the rooms within, appeared to be standing open. There were rays of
      candlelight from one of them, and there was the sound of a footstep going
      about. There were two voices. The words they uttered were not
      distinguishable, but they were both the voices of men. In a few moments
      the voices were silent, and there was no sound of footstep, and the inner
      light went out. If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him
      awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke
      of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of
      the night.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

‘However, a sociable word or two on these mistakes became an easy

      much of it true, and how much of it false—that had its likeness to

      degrees and means, he came to the knowledge of my uneasiness of mind, and
      of its setting at that time in the direction of desiring to see and form
      some judgment of my allotted wife, before she could possibly know me for
      myself; also to try Mrs Boffin and give her a glad surprise. So the plot
      was made out of our getting common sailors’ dresses (as he was able to
      guide me about London), and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer’s
      neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way, and doing whatever
      chance might favour on the spot, and seeing what came of it. If nothing
      came of it, I should be no worse off, and there would merely be a short

‘The child’s father is employed by the house that employs me; that’s how I

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities

      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’

How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now,

      countenance visible in the room; for, Sloppy lightly trotted out with him
      and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street
      door. Mr Sloppy’s instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road;
      but, a scavenger’s cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with
      its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to
      resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart’s contents.
